title: Circular Motion and Simple Harmonic Motion

toc.title: 5.1 Angular quantities; centripetal acceleration and force
5.2 Motion in a horizontal and in a vertical circle
5.3 Simple harmonic motion: displacement, velocity, acceleration, restoring force, energy, period and frequency
5.4 Simple pendulum and spring–mass system; forced oscillation and resonance

html:
Circular motion and simple harmonic motion (SHM) are the two great repeating motions of mechanics, and they are close relatives: SHM is the shadow of uniform circular motion on a diameter. Of the 10 Mechanics questions (official weightage), we estimate about 2 come from this chapter. The favourites are the minimum speed in a vertical circle, banking and friction on curved roads, the velocity and acceleration of SHM at a given displacement, energy in SHM, and how the period of a pendulum or a spring changes — on the Moon, in a lift, or with a cut spring.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • v = r\omega, \omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f; centripetal acceleration v^2/r = \omega^2r towards the centre; it does no work.
  • Level road v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu rg}; banking \tan\theta = v^2/rg; hump of a bridge v = \sqrt{gr}.
  • Vertical circle on a string: v_{top} \ge \sqrt{gr}, v_{bottom} \ge \sqrt{5gr}; T_{bottom} - T_{top} = 6mg.
  • SHM: a = -\omega^2x; v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}; v_{max} = A\omega, a_{max} = A\omega^2; phases 0, \pi/2, \pi.
  • Energy \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2; KE = PE at x = A/\sqrt{2}; energy oscillates at twice the frequency.
  • T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g} and T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}: what each depends on, and springs in series and parallel.
  • Forced oscillation and resonance: amplitude is largest when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency.

5.1 Angular quantities; centripetal acceleration and force

Angular quantities

Quantity Definition SI unit Link with linear quantity
Angular displacement \theta angle swept by the radius: \theta = s/r rad arc s = r\theta
Angular velocity \omega \omega = d\theta/dt; uniform: \omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f rad s⁻¹ v = r\omega
Angular acceleration \alpha \alpha = d\omega/dt rad s⁻² tangential a_t = r\alpha
Time period T / frequency f time for one revolution / revolutions per second s / Hz f = 1/T

1 revolution = 2π rad = 360°. For a machine turning at N rpm, \omega = 2\pi N/60 rad s⁻¹. Hands of a clock: second hand 2\pi/60 rad s⁻¹, minute hand 2\pi/3600, hour hand 2\pi/43\,200 (ratios 60 : 1 between second and minute hands, 12 : 1 between minute and hour hands). The Earth spins at about 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ rad s⁻¹. All points of a rigid rotating body have the same \omega but speeds v = r\omega that grow with distance from the axis.

Centripetal acceleration and force

In uniform circular motion the speed is constant but the direction of the velocity changes all the time, so the body accelerates. The acceleration points along the radius towards the centre (centripetal) and has magnitude

a_c = \frac{v^2}{r} = \omega^2r = v\omega

By the second law there must be a net inward force, the centripetal force:

F_c = \frac{mv^2}{r} = m\omega^2r

The centripetal force is not a new kind of force: it is whichever real force (or resultant) points to the centre — the tension in a string, friction on a turning car, gravity on a satellite, the electric pull on an electron in Bohr's atom, the normal reaction of a wall.

In uniform circular motion Constant?
speed, kinetic energy, angular velocity, magnitude of acceleration yes
velocity, linear momentum, acceleration (directions change) no
angular momentum about the centre yes
work done by the centripetal force always zero (force ⟂ velocity)

If the speed also changes (non-uniform circular motion), there is a tangential acceleration a_t = dv/dt as well, and the total acceleration is \sqrt{a_c^2 + a_t^2}.

Centrifugal force

"Centrifugal force" mv^2/r, pointing outward, appears only to an observer in the rotating frame — it is a pseudo force, not the reaction to the centripetal force. When the string of a whirling stone breaks, the stone flies off along the tangent, not radially outward.

Worked example 5.1 — a whirled stone

Problem. A 0.5 kg stone tied to a 1 m string is whirled in a horizontal circle at 2 revolutions per second. Find its speed, its acceleration and the tension (ignore gravity's effect on the string).

Solution. \omega = 2\pi f = 4\pi rad s⁻¹; v = r\omega = 4\pi = 12.6 m s⁻¹; a = \omega^2r = 16\pi^2 = 158 m s⁻²; T = ma = 79 N. Doubling the rate of turning would make the tension four times as large.

5.2 Motion in a horizontal and in a vertical circle

Horizontal circles

Situation Force supplying mv^2/r Result
Car on a level curved road friction, \mu mg at most v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu rg} (independent of mass)
Road banked at angle \theta, no friction needed horizontal component of the normal reaction, N\sin\theta \tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}
Banked road with friction \mu normal reaction and friction together v_{max} = \sqrt{rg\frac{\mu + \tan\theta}{1 - \mu\tan\theta}}
Cyclist rounding a bend friction; he leans inward at angle \theta from the vertical \tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}
Conical pendulum (string length L at angle \theta to vertical) horizontal component of tension: T\sin\theta = mv^2/r, T\cos\theta = mg \tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}; period 2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g}
Rider on the vertical wall of a "well of death" normal reaction of the wall; friction \mu N holds up the weight v_{min} = \sqrt{rg/\mu}

Banking lets vehicles turn without depending on friction, which is why outer edges of curves on highways and railway tracks (the outer rail) are raised.

Vertical circle

A body of mass m on a string of length r whirled in a vertical circle: gravity helps at the top and opposes at the bottom, and the speed changes around the circle (energy conservation: v_{bottom}^2 = v_{top}^2 + 4gr).

Point of the circle (string) Tension Least speed to complete the loop
Top T_{top} = \frac{mv_{top}^2}{r} - mg \sqrt{gr} (string just slack, T_{top} = 0)
Horizontal (side) T = \frac{mv^2}{r} \sqrt{3gr}
Bottom T_{bottom} = \frac{mv_{bottom}^2}{r} + mg \sqrt{5gr}
Difference T_{bottom} - T_{top} = 6mg (for any speed that completes the loop)

If the body is on a light rigid rod instead of a string, the rod can push as well as pull, so the body need only reach the top: v_{top} \ge 0 and v_{bottom} \ge \sqrt{4gr} = 2\sqrt{gr}. A bucket of water swung in a vertical circle does not spill if v_{top} \ge \sqrt{gr} — at that speed the water's weight alone supplies the centripetal force.

Over a hump and through a dip. A car at the top of a convex bridge of radius r: N = mg - mv^2/r (it feels lighter), and it leaves the road when v = \sqrt{gr}. At the bottom of a dip: N = mg + mv^2/r (it presses harder). A pilot pulling out of a dive feels the same extra weight.

Worked example 5.2 — roads and loops

Problem. (g = 10 m s⁻²) (a) Find the greatest speed of a car on a level curve of radius 100 m if \mu = 0.4. (b) At what angle should a curve of radius 45 m be banked for 15 m s⁻¹? (c) A 0.2 kg stone on a 1 m string has speed 8 m s⁻¹ at the bottom of a vertical circle. Find its speed and the tension at the top, and the tension at the bottom.

Solution. (a) v = \sqrt{\mu rg} = \sqrt{400} = 20 m s⁻¹ = 72 km h⁻¹. (b) \tan\theta = 225/450 = 0.5, \theta = 26.6^{\circ}. (c) v_{top}^2 = 64 - 4(10)(1) = 24, v_{top} = 4.9 m s⁻¹ (above \sqrt{gr} = 3.2, so the loop is completed). T_{top} = 0.2(24) - 2 = 2.8 N; T_{bottom} = 0.2(64) + 2 = 14.8 N. The difference, 12 N, is 6mg.

5.3 Simple harmonic motion: displacement, velocity, acceleration, restoring force, energy, period and frequency

Simple harmonic motion

A body executes simple harmonic motion when its acceleration (equivalently, the restoring force on it) is directly proportional to its displacement from a fixed mean position and always directed towards that position: F = -kx, a = -\omega^2x.

The solution of a = -\omega^2x is

x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi)

Term Meaning
A amplitude — the greatest displacement from the mean position
\omega t + \phi phase — tells the position and direction of motion at time t
\phi initial phase (epoch) — the phase at t = 0
\omega = \sqrt{k/m} angular frequency (rad s⁻¹)
T = 2\pi/\omega period; f = 1/T = \omega/2\pi is the frequency (Hz)

Every SHM is periodic, but not every periodic motion is SHM (the Earth's orbit, a bouncing ball). SHM is the projection of uniform circular motion on a diameter: a point moving round a circle of radius A at angular speed \omega has a shadow on a diameter that moves exactly as x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi).

Velocity and acceleration

v = \frac{dx}{dt} = A\omega\cos(\omega t + \phi) = \pm\,\omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}, \qquad a = -\omega^2x

At the mean position (x = 0) At an extreme (x = \pm A)
Speed maximum, v_{max} = A\omega zero
Acceleration and restoring force zero maximum, a_{max} = A\omega^2, F_{max} = kA
Kinetic energy maximum zero
Potential energy zero (minimum) maximum

Phase relations: velocity leads displacement by \pi/2; acceleration leads velocity by \pi/2; acceleration and displacement are in antiphase (\pi apart). The v–x graph is an ellipse (a circle if v is plotted in units of \omega); the a–x graph is a straight line of slope -\omega^2 through the origin.

Energy in SHM

With k = m\omega^2:

K = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2(A^2 - x^2), \qquad U = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2x^2, \qquad E = K + U = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2

The total energy is constant and proportional to the square of the amplitude and to the square of the frequency. K = U when x = A/\sqrt{2}. At x = A/2, U = E/4 and K = 3E/4. Kinetic and potential energy each vary periodically with twice the frequency of the motion (period T/2), because each reaches its maximum twice per cycle.

Worked example 5.3 — reading an SHM equation

Problem. A particle moves as x = 0.1\sin(4\pi t) (metres, seconds). Find the amplitude, frequency, period, maximum speed and maximum acceleration.

Solution. A = 0.1 m; \omega = 4\pi rad s⁻¹, so f = \omega/2\pi = 2 Hz and T = 0.5 s. v_{max} = A\omega = 0.4\pi = 1.26 m s⁻¹; a_{max} = A\omega^2 = 1.6\pi^2 = 15.8 m s⁻².

Time inside one oscillation

From the mean position, the particle reaches x = A/2 in T/12 (since \sin\omega t = \frac{1}{2} at \omega t = \pi/6) and then needs another T/6 to reach x = A. It moves fastest near the middle and slowly near the ends — so a pendulum spends most of its time near the extremes.

Worked example — reading a turning point from an SHM energy split

A particle in SHM has total energy 16 J. At a displacement of half the amplitude (x = A/2), find the kinetic and potential energies.

Potential energy varies as x² and equals the total at x = A, so at A/2 it is (1/2)² = ¼ of the total: PE = 4 J, KE = 12 J. The same square law settles the favourite variants: KE = PE when x = A/√2 (≈ 0.71A, not at A/2), and at x = A/√2 the speed is vmax/√2. Most wrong answers here come from treating PE as proportional to x instead of x².

Trap — what the pendulum's period ignores

T = 2π√(l/g) contains no mass and no amplitude (for small swings): a heavier bob or a slightly wider swing does not change the period — the two most common distractors in this unit. What does change it: length, g (longer on the Moon/top of a mountain, shorter in a lift accelerating upward... where effective g becomes g + a) and, for the spring–mass system instead, the mass and the spring constant.

5.4 Simple pendulum and spring–mass system; forced oscillation and resonance

Simple pendulum

A point mass (bob) on a light, inextensible string of length l, displaced by a small angle \theta, feels a restoring force mg\sin\theta \approx mg\theta = mg\,x/l along its arc. This is SHM with \omega^2 = g/l:

T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{l}{g}}

valid for small amplitudes (a few degrees). T does not depend on the mass of the bob, nor (for small swings) on the amplitude — the isochronism of the pendulum. l is measured from the point of suspension to the centre of the bob.

Change Effect on T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}
Length × 4 T × 2 (T \propto \sqrt{l})
Heavier bob, same length no change
On the Moon (g/6) T \times \sqrt{6} \approx 2.45
Lift accelerating up at a (or descending and slowing) T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/(g + a)} — shorter
Lift accelerating down at a T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/(g - a)} — longer
Freely falling lift or orbiting satellite no restoring force: no oscillation (T \to \infty)
Summer (metal rod expands) l rises, T rises: a pendulum clock loses time
Clock taken up Mount Everest or down a deep mine g smaller, T longer: the clock loses time

The seconds pendulum has a period of 2 s (each swing 1 s); its length is l = gT^2/4\pi^2 \approx 0.99 m for g = 9.8 m s⁻² (exactly 1 m if g = \pi^2 m s⁻²).

Spring–mass system

A mass m on a spring of force constant k (Hooke's law F = -kx):

T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{m}{k}}, \qquad f = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{\frac{k}{m}}

  • T does not depend on g: the same on the Moon, in a lift or on a slope (horizontal or vertical spring alike).
  • For a vertical spring with static extension e = mg/k: T = 2\pi\sqrt{e/g}.
  • To double T, put on four times the mass.
Springs combined Effective force constant Period with mass m
Two springs k_1, k_2 in series \frac{1}{k} = \frac{1}{k_1} + \frac{1}{k_2} (two equal: k/2) larger (\sqrt{2}T for two equal)
Two springs in parallel k = k_1 + k_2 (two equal: 2k) smaller (T/\sqrt{2} for two equal)
Spring cut into n equal pieces each piece has nk (half a spring is twice as stiff) one piece: T/\sqrt{n}
Worked example 5.4 — pendulum and spring

Problem. (a) A pendulum beats exactly 2 s on Earth. What is its period on the Moon, where g is one-sixth? (b) A 1 kg mass on a spring of force constant 400 N m⁻¹. Find the period. (c) A mass hung on a vertical spring stretches it by 9.8 cm. Find the period of vertical oscillation (g = 9.8 m s⁻²).

Solution. (a) T \propto 1/\sqrt{g}: 2\sqrt{6} = 4.9 s. (b) T = 2\pi\sqrt{1/400} = \pi/10 = 0.31 s. (c) T = 2\pi\sqrt{e/g} = 2\pi\sqrt{0.098/9.8} = 2\pi(0.1) = 0.63 s. A spring clock would keep the same time on the Moon; a pendulum clock would not.

Pendulum versus spring

T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g} depends on g but not on mass; T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} depends on mass but not on g. Options that mix these up — "the pendulum's period doubles if the mass is doubled", "the spring's period changes on the Moon" — are the usual traps.

Damped, free and forced oscillations; resonance

  • Free (natural) oscillation: a system displaced and released oscillates at its own natural frequency f_0, fixed by its build (\sqrt{k/m}/2\pi or \sqrt{g/l}/2\pi).
  • Damped oscillation: friction and air resistance take energy away, so the amplitude decreases with time (the frequency stays almost the same). Shock absorbers in vehicles damp the oscillations of the springs on purpose.
  • Forced oscillation: a periodic external force drives the system; after a while it oscillates at the frequency of the driving force, not at its own.
  • Resonance: when the driving frequency equals (or is very close to) the natural frequency, the system absorbs energy most readily and the amplitude becomes maximum. The smaller the damping, the taller and sharper the resonance peak.

Examples of resonance: a swing pushed in step with its own rhythm goes higher and higher; soldiers break step when marching across a suspension bridge so that their rhythm cannot drive it at its natural frequency; a singer's sustained note at the right pitch can shatter a wine glass; a radio or TV set is tuned by adjusting the natural frequency of its circuit to that of the station (electrical resonance, Chapter 16); in an earthquake, buildings whose natural frequency matches the frequency of the ground shaking sway most violently.

Formula and fact sheet

Topic Formula or fact
Angular quantities \theta = s/r; \omega = 2\pi/T = 2\pi f = 2\pi N/60; v = r\omega; a_t = r\alpha
Centripetal a = v^2/r = \omega^2r = v\omega; F = mv^2/r; does no work
Level road v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu rg}
Banking / cyclist / conical pendulum \tan\theta = v^2/rg; conical pendulum T = 2\pi\sqrt{L\cos\theta/g}
Banked road with friction v_{max} = \sqrt{rg(\mu + \tan\theta)/(1 - \mu\tan\theta)}
Hump / dip N = mg \mp mv^2/r; leaves a hump at v = \sqrt{gr}
Vertical circle (string) v_{top} \ge \sqrt{gr}, v_{side} \ge \sqrt{3gr}, v_{bottom} \ge \sqrt{5gr}; T_b - T_t = 6mg
Vertical circle (rod) v_{bottom} \ge 2\sqrt{gr}
SHM a = -\omega^2x; x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi); v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}
SHM maxima v_{max} = A\omega (mean position); a_{max} = A\omega^2 (extremes)
Phases v leads x by \pi/2; a and x differ by \pi
SHM energy E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2 = \frac{1}{2}kA^2; K = U at A/\sqrt{2}; energies vary at 2f
Simple pendulum T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g}; seconds pendulum T = 2 s, l \approx 0.99 m; in lift g \to g \pm a
Spring–mass T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} = 2\pi\sqrt{e/g}; series 1/k = 1/k_1 + 1/k_2; parallel k_1 + k_2; n pieces nk each
Resonance driving frequency = natural frequency → maximum amplitude; less damping, sharper peak

Chapter summary

  • In uniform circular motion speed is constant but velocity is not; the acceleration v^2/r = \omega^2r points to the centre, and the centripetal force does no work.
  • The centripetal force is supplied by a real force: friction on a level road (v_{max} = \sqrt{\mu rg}), the normal reaction on a banked road (\tan\theta = v^2/rg), tension, gravity.
  • In a vertical circle on a string the least speeds are \sqrt{gr} at the top and \sqrt{5gr} at the bottom; the tension is greatest at the bottom, by 6mg more than at the top.
  • SHM: acceleration = -\omega^2\times displacement; x = A\sin(\omega t + \phi), v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2}; speed is greatest at the mean position, acceleration at the extremes.
  • Total energy \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2 is constant; KE = PE at x = A/\sqrt{2}; each form of energy oscillates at twice the frequency.
  • Simple pendulum T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g} (independent of mass, depends on g); spring T = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k} (depends on mass, independent of g).
  • Springs in series are softer, in parallel stiffer; half a spring is twice as stiff.
  • Forced oscillations take the driver's frequency; at resonance (driving frequency = natural frequency) the amplitude is greatest, more sharply so with less damping.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (a) — angle (radian) per second. rad s⁻² is angular acceleration.

2. (c) — the direction of motion changes all the time, so velocity, momentum and the acceleration vector change; only the speed (and KE) stay constant.

3. (d) — a = v^2/r = \omega^2r.

4. (b) — it is centre-seeking (centripetal); the velocity is along the tangent.

5. (c) — the force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant, so it does no work in any part of the motion.

6. (a) — it is a fictitious force felt in a rotating (non-inertial) frame; the centripetal force has no outward "reaction" acting on the same body.

7. (b) — at the top the string is just slack when mg = mv^2/r, giving v = \sqrt{gr}. Zero is the answer for a rigid rod.

8. (d) — energy: v_b^2 = v_t^2 + 4gr = gr + 4gr = 5gr.

9. (a) — N\cos\theta = mg and N\sin\theta = mv^2/r; dividing, \tan\theta = v^2/rg.

10. (c) — friction supplies the centripetal force: \mu mg = mv^2/r, so v = \sqrt{\mu rg}.

11. (b) — the defining condition of SHM: a = -\omega^2x.

12. (d) — v = \omega\sqrt{A^2 - x^2} is greatest, A\omega, at x = 0.

13. (a) — |a| = \omega^2|x| is greatest, A\omega^2, at x = \pm A, where the particle is momentarily at rest.

14. (d) — a = -\omega^2x: acceleration is always opposite to displacement, a phase difference of \pi.

15. (b) — E = \frac{1}{2}m\omega^2A^2; double the amplitude, four times the energy.

16. (b) — T = 2\pi\sqrt{l/g} for small swings. (a) has l and g the wrong way round: \sqrt{l/g} has the unit of time, \sqrt{g/l} of frequency.

17. (d) — \omega = \sqrt{k/m}, so T = 2\pi/\omega = 2\pi\sqrt{m/k}.

18. (a) — a seconds pendulum takes 1 s for each swing, so its full period is 2 s.

19. (c) — at resonance the driver is in step with the natural oscillation and the amplitude is greatest.

20. (b) — resistive forces remove energy, so the amplitude dies away; the frequency changes very little.

21. (c) — v = A\omega\cos(\omega t + \phi) = A\omega\sin(\omega t + \phi + \pi/2): velocity leads displacement by \pi/2.

22. (d) — one revolution is 2\pi rad in time T, so \omega = 2\pi/T.

Answers and explanations — Set B
